Most police recorded crime statistics are official statistics rather than accredited official statistics; accreditation was removed in 2014; unlawful-death statistics based on the Homicide Index were restored separately.
Designation varies by product; accreditation status is not a parcel-confidence score.
Data originate from 43 territorial forces plus British Transport Police; returns are derived from local force record-management systems; notifiable-offence data are supplied monthly.
Local systems differ; monthly supply does not prove uniform recording quality.
Home Office Crime Analysis Unit quality assures the force data; final data are sent to ONS at quarter end; ONS publishes aggregate statistics quarterly and annually.
Quarterly publication lags operational recording; aggregate publication cannot reproduce record-level QA.

Statistics are published on a rolling 12-month basis; national, Police Force Area and Community Safety Partnership levels are available; reports are typically published within four months of the period.
PFA and CSP are not LSOA or parcel geographies; publication timeliness is not event timeliness.

NCRS was introduced across England and Wales in April 2002; it uses a victim-oriented approach; an allegation meeting the legal test is recorded unless credible contrary evidence is immediately available.
Recording rules create time-series breaks; the rule does not prove every local decision was correct.
Police recorded crime is administrative data; quality is affected by recording rules and systems; human error and operational resource decisions can affect figures.
Observed changes may mix crime and process effects; factors vary across forces.
Proactive policing can increase recorded drug or weapon offences; the increase may occur without a matching change in underlying crime; commentary and caveats are required for trends.
Activity effects differ by offence; not suitable as a direct safety score.
Changes in recording practices affect violent and sexual offence trends; improved NCRS compliance increased recorded counts; the scale and force variation cannot be fully quantified.
Recorded figures may be better indicators of police activity than underlying trends; historical comparisons require caveats.
The 2025 summary reports 94.8 percent for all crime excluding fraud; 93.6 percent for violent crime; 95.9 percent for sexual offences.
National estimates are not force or parcel values; inspection sampling uncertainty remains relevant.
Each force is scheduled for crime-data-integrity inspection in the 2025 to 2027 PEEL round; inspection findings support quality interpretation; inspection timing is not continuous.
Coverage does not imply simultaneous observation; inspection evidence must be dated.
Forces no longer receive a graded crime-data-integrity judgment; HMICFRS uses a dip sample of files; relevant findings feed other PEEL core questions.
Dip samples are not full audits; absence of a grade is not evidence of perfect recording.
Concerns about crime recording can trigger a full crime-data-integrity audit; routine dip sampling and full audit are distinct; escalation is risk-based.
No escalation does not certify every record; audit scope and date must be retained.
The data quality framework rates offence trend reliability; ratings use good, moderate or poor classes; criteria differ for CSEW and police recorded crime.
Ratings are offence-level not parcel-level; classes should not be converted to numeric safety.
Homicide trend reliability is rated good; knife or sharp instrument offence reliability is rated moderate; recommended source differs by offence.
